analysis.one_liner: Keeps copyright on private technical standards that governments make into law, as long as they're viewable free online.
analysis.headline: The House defeated the bill on July 22, 2024, 248–127, falling short of the two-thirds majority required to pass it under the fast-track procedure used.
analysis.plain_summary: Governments routinely write private technical standards — building codes, electrical codes, fire codes — into law without copying them into the statute, a practice called incorporation by reference. Some courts have ruled that a standard becomes public-domain law once incorporated; the Pro Codes Act would overturn that by law, declaring the standards stay copyrighted even after incorporation. In exchange, the standards body would have to make the standard viewable free online. Reading the law would be free, but copying, printing, or republishing it would remain licensed — and the burden would fall on the public to prove the standards body failed to comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Standards development organizations — the private bodies that write the codes governments turn into law, such as building-code and fire-code publishers. The bill would have locked in their copyright and their revenue from selling and licensing the standards that federal, state, and local law makes binding — over 23,000 sections of federal regulations incorporate such standards. It would also have protected them in court by placing the burden of proof on anyone challenging their compliance with the free-access requirement.

how_it_helps.text: A standard incorporated by reference into law would retain its copyright protection if the standards body makes it viewable free online, securing the organizations' sales and licensing revenue from industries and professionals.
If a party argues the organization failed to keep the standard publicly accessible, that party bears the burden of proving noncompliance, making challenges harder to win.

The committee-added version required free online access in a searchable format — a concession to public-access concerns — and directed the Copyright Office and GAO to study effects on consumers, disadvantaged communities, homeowners, small businesses, First Amendment rights, and free online code platforms.

analysis.who_pays: Anyone who must obey a privately written standard that has become law: homeowners and contractors who need the building and safety codes behind permits, small businesses facing compliance burdens, and state and local governments paying fees for access to standards they are legally required to enforce. Online platforms that publish legal codes for free would have faced renewed copyright exposure. Free online viewing would have been guaranteed, but only in read-only form — no printing, copying, or sharing without a license.
analysis.who_pays_short: Homeowners, contractors, small businesses, local governments

drawbacks.text: Standards that private bodies wrote would remain copyrighted even after governments make them binding law, so the law itself would stay partly a licensed product — viewable for free but not printable, copyable, or redistributable.
The bill reversed a judicial trend toward treating incorporated standards as public-domain law, a shift courts had made because people cannot be bound by rules they cannot read without paying.
State and local governments would keep paying fees to standards organizations for access to rules they must enforce; the bill ordered a study of these costs rather than eliminating them.

The free-access requirement allows requiring users to create accounts and accept terms of service, and critics noted this left room for restrictive conditions — the bill ordered its own GAO study on exactly that concern.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's one real public benefit — a guaranteed right to view any law-bound standard free online — was meaningful, since today some standards are not freely viewable. But the bill's central effect was to settle, in the standards bodies' favor, an open legal question that courts had been resolving toward public access: whether a private standard that becomes law still belongs to the company that wrote it. Viewers get read-only windows; the underlying property right over the law itself stays private. For a measure framed as 'Protecting and Enhancing Public Access to Codes,' the access gains were narrower than the entrenchment.

outcome.mechanism: Supporters brought it to the floor under suspension of the rules — a fast-track procedure that skips amendment debate but requires a two-thirds vote — and it got 248 yes votes, short of the roughly two-thirds needed, so it failed and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House Judiciary Committee reported the bill favorably on a 19–4 vote on July 22, 2024, after adding amendments requiring free online viewing and a series of GAO and Copyright Office studies.
The same day, the House voted 248–127 on passage under suspension of the rules, which requires a two-thirds majority; the bill fell short and was not taken up again before the 118th Congress ended.
Both parties backed the bill by majority — Republicans 143–49 in favor, Democrats 105–78 in favor — but opposition was concentrated among Democrats, which was enough to deny the two-thirds threshold.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Citizens and free-law publishers who read and share building and safety codes online avoided a new copyright layer over rules that are legally binding. The standards organizations, which would have gained a statutory guarantee over their most contested revenue, did not get it — though the underlying legal question remains unsettled in the courts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Citizens who read safety codes online free

for.name: Rep. Darrell Issa
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, moved to suspend the rules and pass it, and carried it through committee.

for.name: Rep. Deborah Ross
for.what_they_did: Co-introduced the bill with Issa, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

for.name: House Judiciary Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill favorably as amended on a 19–4 vote after three markup sessions.

against.name: 78 of 216 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no on passage — the largest single bloc of opposition, and enough combined with Republican defectors to deny the two-thirds vote.

against.name: Open-access and free-law advocates
against.role: Public-access campaigners, including free-law publisher Carl Malamud of Public.Resource.Org
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill as writing copyright protection over the law itself and keeping legally binding codes paywalled from people who need to print and share them.

sides.party_line_note: Both parties voted for the bill by majority — Republicans 143 yes to 49 no, Democrats 105 yes to 78 no — but opposition was concentrated among Democrats, and their no votes kept the bill short of the two-thirds needed.

industries.industry: Standards development organizations (building, fire, electrical code publishers)
industries.note: The bill would have written into federal copyright law that codes these organizations wrote stay copyrighted even after governments make them binding law — protecting sales and subscription revenue from industries and professionals, with public access limited to free read-only viewing. Their gain in locking down the law's text is the public's cost in access to the rules they must obey.

industries.industry: Online platforms that publish legal codes for free
industries.note: By reaffirming copyright in incorporated standards, the bill would have exposed platforms that freely republish codes to infringement risk. The bill's own text ordered a GAO study on how it would affect these platforms' operations, an acknowledgment of the concern.

industries.industry: Homeowners, contractors, and small businesses needing code access
industries.note: Free online viewing would have helped people check the building and safety codes behind permits, but the bill preserved their obligation to buy licensed copies for any use beyond viewing, and ordered studies of homeowner and small-business costs rather than addressing them.
